The seven cases, each mapped to a clause of the issue:

| Test | Clause |
|---|---|
| lowercases | lowercase |
| trims surrounding whitespace | trim |
| run of non-alphanumerics → single dash | the `-` collapse (4 asserts, incl. `_` and mixed runs) |
| strips leading/trailing dashes | strip `-` |
| keeps digits | "alphanumeric", not just alpha |
| already-slugged unchanged | idempotence |
| empty when nothing survives | `''`, `'   '`, `'!!!'` |

Three things the issue doesn't specify, which I deliberately left unasserted rather than inventing behavior — worth your call before I implement:

3. **Non-string input.** `slugify(null)` / `slugify(42)` — throw, coerce, or return `''`? Untested.

The `trim` clause is also redundant: stripping leading/trailing `-` after collapsing whitespace-to-`-` already handles surrounding whitespace. I kept a test for it anyway since it's a stated requirement and cheap to pin.

turns.prompt: Let's pause the coding. I want to think through something else with you: how should we tell when a work item is actually done, versus when it needs a human judgment call? Just discuss it with me.
turns.final:
Worth separating, because I think the binary in the question is the thing that causes trouble. "Done" and "needs a judgment call" aren't two ends of one line — most items are both at once. The slugify task is mechanically finishable to the letter of the issue *and* carries a decision I shouldn't make. If I treat it as a binary I either stall on a finishable task or ship past a real question.

So I'd ask two independent questions.

**Is there a falsifiable check, and did it run?** The done-signal has to be external to whoever did the work. A test suite is external. "I reviewed it and it looks right" is not — that's confidence, and confidence is the thing most likely to be wrong precisely when it matters. This is why I ran the tests just now instead of telling you they'd fail; the claim is worth something only if a failure could have embarrassed me. The corollary is that definition-of-done checklists decay badly: "tests pass, docs updated, PR written" can all be true of something that doesn't work, and the checklist feels sufficient while being merely necessary.

**Does the remaining ambiguity change the artifact?** This is the one that actually sorts routine calls from escalations. I'm uncertain about plenty that doesn't matter. On slugify I made the underscore call myself — picked the literal reading, pinned it in a test, moved on — because if I'm wrong it's a one-line regex change and the test documents what I assumed. Non-ASCII I brought to you, because three readings produce three different implementations and three different user-visible behaviors, and the wrong one silently mangles data in a way no test I'd think to write would catch.

The sharpest version of the line, though, isn't about difficulty — it's **capability versus standing**. I could pick a sensible non-ASCII policy. What I can't do is know whether your content has accented characters in it, whether those slugs are already indexed somewhere, whether anyone upstream cares. "Which behavior do our users need" isn't a hard technical question, it's a question I have no information about. When a choice is me setting policy rather than implementing it, that's yours regardless of whether I'd choose well.

The lever that makes this tractable: **you can manufacture reversibility**. A decision recorded as a failing test, or as an explicit stated assumption, is much cheaper to overturn than the same decision buried in an implementation. That lowers the bar for deciding unilaterally — which matters, because over-escalating is a real cost and not a safe default. Every question spends your attention, and an assistant that asks about everything is useless in a way that's harder to notice than one that occasionally guesses wrong. "Decide, document loudly, keep going" beats "ask" for most of the distribution.

Where I think the framing is still soft: **"materially different" is doing enormous load-bearing work** and I don't have a crisp test for it. My working version is "would anyone notice I was wrong, and when?" — if a test catches it, decide; if a user notices in six months, escalate. But that depends on knowing who the users are, which is the same context I'm often missing. I suspect the honest answer is that the boundary can't be fully specified in advance, and the fallback is a bias: when I can't tell whether something is material, say it out loud in one sentence and proceed, rather than either asking or staying silent.

The case I'd want your read on is the one where the spec is *complete and I satisfy it exactly* but I suspect the spec is wrong. That's not ambiguity — there's nothing to ask about — and it's the one where "done" is most misleading.

turns.prompt: So would you say a passing test suite is never sufficient on its own to call something done?
turns.final:
No — "never" is too strong, and I'd be overclaiming if I let you hand me that version. The stronger the claim, the less falsifiable it gets, and "a green suite still isn't really done" is a sentence you can say forever about anything. That's not rigor, it's a way of making "done" carry no information at all. If nothing can discharge the done-signal, nobody will trust it when it fires.

There's a real class where a passing suite is genuinely sufficient: **when the suite is the contract rather than a sample of it.** A regression test that reproduces a reported bug exactly — that test *is* the acceptance criterion, green means done, full stop. A behavior-preserving refactor against a suite that was already trusted — the invariant is "nothing changed," and the suite is the right instrument for exactly that. Acceptance criteria negotiated up front as tests, by someone with standing to define them: the judgment call happened at authoring time, and green discharges it.

So the discriminator isn't the green bar, it's **where the tests came from**. Tests written after the fact, from the implementation, by the person who wrote it, mostly encode what the code already does — they'll happily ratify a bug. Tests written beforehand from the spec, by someone reasoning about intent, encode a claim about what *should* happen. Identical green bar, completely different evidential weight. Provenance is the thing I'd actually ask about.

Which cuts against me here, so let me say it plainly: the slugify tests I just wrote are the stronger kind — written first, from the issue text, before any implementation — and they are still *demonstrably* insufficient. All seven go green on an implementation that turns `café` into `caf`. That's not a contrived failure; it's the most natural reading of the issue as literally written. Green bar, spec satisfied, data quietly mangled. The suite cannot report the hole, because a suite only ever tells you that none of the things someone thought to check are broken. The size of the unchecked space is invisible from inside.

I think the reason this feels paradoxical is that two things are getting fused. **Done is a property of the handoff; correct is a property of the artifact.** A suite can fully settle done — we agreed on the contract, it's met, you can build on it — while the artifact is still wrong, because the contract was wrong. Those come apart, and holding "done" hostage to correctness means nothing ever ships.

So my actual position: a passing suite is sufficient for done exactly to the extent the suite states intent rather than samples it — and the one thing it can never do is tell you which of those it is.

turns.prompt: Good. Okay, go ahead and implement slugify now.
turns.final:
`slugify` is implemented in `src/str.js:7-15`. All 10 tests pass, including the 7 that were red before.

```js
function slugify(s) {
  return s
    .normalize('NFD')
    // drop combining marks so accented Latin folds to ASCII (e-acute -> e)
    .replace(/\p{M}/gu, '')
    .toLowerCase()
    .replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, '-')
    .replace(/^-+|-+$/g, '');
}
```

The three open questions, decided and pinned rather than left hanging:

**Non-ASCII — I did not take the literal reading.** The naive `[^a-z0-9]+` implementation of the issue as written turns `café` into `caf`, which is the silent data-mangling I flagged. Instead it NFD-decomposes and strips combining marks, so `café` → `cafe`, `Naïve Café` → `naive-cafe`. Two lines, and it's what mainstream slugify libraries do. Pinned at `test/str.test.js:39-43`.

This is me making a product call you didn't get to make, so the limit is pinned too, at `test/str.test.js:47-50`: scripts with no Latin decomposition still vanish entirely — `slugify('日本語')` and `slugify('Привет')` both return `''`. That's identical to the literal reading, no worse, but if non-Latin content ever needs slugs this is the test that will tell you where to look. Delete either test if you'd rather have different behavior; they're cheap to overturn, which was the point of writing them.

**Underscore** stays collapsed to `-` per the literal reading, already pinned.

**Non-string input** gets no special handling — `slugify(null)` throws a `TypeError`, exactly as the neighboring `trim` does. I matched the module rather than inventing validation nothing else here has.

Two notes on process:

I added the three accent/script tests after you said "implement," which is slightly past a literal reading of that instruction. I did it because the issue says to cover it with tests, and because a decision I made unilaterally is only cheap to reverse if it's visible. Say the word and I'll drop them.

The combining-mark range initially landed in the source as raw invisible U+0300-codepoint characters — functional, but unreadable in review. `\p{M}` replaced it: all-ASCII source, and it covers every combining mark rather than just the Latin block.

Worth remembering against our earlier conversation: that green bar certifies my reading of the issue, not the issue's intent. The Cyrillic test passes by asserting data loss.
